cards.front: An organism's {{c1::life history}} is its schedule: how fast it grows, when it first breeds, how many offspring it makes and how large they are, how often it breeds, and how long it lives.
cards.quote: An organism's life history is its schedule: how fast it grows, when it first breeds, how many offspring it makes and how large they are

cards.front: In evolutionary ecology, what is fitness, and what is one common measure of it?
cards.back: An individual's contribution to future generations relative to others in the same environment. One common measure is lifetime reproductive success: offspring produced over its life, often counted as those that survive to breed.
cards.quote: Fitness is an individual's contribution to future generations relative to others in the same environment

cards.front: In life-history theory, what is the difference between acquisition and allocation?
cards.back: Acquisition is what an individual takes in and can use; allocation is how it splits that intake among uses.
cards.quote: Acquisition is what an individual takes in and can use; allocation is how it splits that among uses.

cards.front: A {{c1::trade-off}} is the negative link allocation creates: for one individual, more to one use leaves less for another.
cards.quote: A trade-off is the negative link allocation creates: for one individual, more to one use leaves less for another.

cards.front: In life-history theory, what sets the size of an individual's budget, where do trade-offs live, and which split of the budget does selection favour?
cards.back: Intake sets the budget. Trade-offs live in how it is split among growth, upkeep, storage and reproduction. Selection favours the split that leaves the most descendants, given who dies at what age.
cards.quote: and selection favours whichever split leaves the most descendants, given who dies at what age.

cards.front: Why is "one fixed energy budget" treated as a model to test, not a law, in life-history work?
cards.back: Some costs run through particular nutrients, and a manipulation can show that extra breeding costs something without showing a fixed budget is the reason: parents may forage harder.
cards.quote: a manipulation can show that extra breeding costs something without showing that one fixed budget is why (parents may forage harder)

cards.front: {{c1::Semelparity}} is a single reproductive episode in a lifetime, usually followed by death, as in most Pacific salmon and century plants.
cards.back: Its opposite, repeated reproduction, is iteroparity.
cards.quote: Semelparity is a single reproductive episode in a lifetime, usually followed by death
cards.section: Semelparity, iteroparity and the cost of reproduction

cards.front: {{c1::Iteroparity}} is repeated reproduction, as in most birds, mammals and long-lived trees.
cards.quote: Iteroparity is repeated reproduction, as in most birds, mammals and long-lived trees.
cards.section: Semelparity, iteroparity and the cost of reproduction

cards.front: "A salmon dies because it spent everything on spawning." Why is this not an evolutionary explanation of semelparity?
cards.back: It is a physiological description. The evolutionary question is comparative: did individuals that put more into one bout leave more descendants than those that held some back to breed again?
cards.quote: is a physiological description, not an evolutionary explanation.
cards.section: Semelparity, iteroparity and the cost of reproduction

cards.front: In the simplest annual model (juvenile survival c, adult survival p, same age at first breeding), what does each type leave per year, and what break-even rule follows?
cards.back: Repeat breeder: c × b₂ breeding young plus itself with probability p. Once-breeder: c × b₁ and dies. Break even when c × b₁ = c × b₂ + p, so b₁ − b₂ = p / c.
cards.quote: Each year a repeat breeder that makes b₂ young leaves c × b₂ young that will breed, plus itself with probability p.
cards.section: Semelparity, iteroparity and the cost of reproduction

cards.front: In the simple annual model where a once-breeder needs b₁ − b₂ = p / c extra young to break even, adult survival p = 0.8 and juvenile survival c = 0.1. How many extra young are needed? What if p = 0.2 and c = 0.4?
cards.back: p / c = 0.8 / 0.1 = 8 extra young. With p = 0.2 and c = 0.4, p / c = 0.5 extra young, a much lower bar.
cards.why: High adult survival makes staying alive to breed again worth a lot; high juvenile survival makes each extra young worth a lot.
cards.quote: They break even when c × b₁ = c × b₂ + p.
cards.section: Semelparity, iteroparity and the cost of reproduction

cards.front: Using the break-even rule b₁ − b₂ = p / c, under which combination of adult survival (p) and juvenile survival (c) should breeding once be easiest to favour, and why?
cards.back: Low adult survival with high juvenile survival. That makes p / c small, so a once-breeder needs few extra young to match a repeat breeder.
cards.why: A repeat breeder's advantage is surviving to breed again (p); each extra young is worth c.
cards.quote: Call c the chance that a newborn survives to breed (juvenile survival) and p the chance that an adult survives a year (adult survival).
cards.section: Semelparity, iteroparity and the cost of reproduction

cards.front: The simple annual model of breeding once versus repeatedly leaves out year-to-year change. What do models predict where juvenile survival varies a lot between years?
cards.back: Repeated breeding can also pay.
cards.quote: where the survival of young varies a lot from year to year, models predict that repeated breeding can also pay.
cards.section: Semelparity, iteroparity and the cost of reproduction

cards.front: The {{c1::cost of reproduction}} is the reduction in survival or future reproduction that follows from reproducing now.
cards.quote: The cost of reproduction is the reduction in survival or future reproduction that follows from reproducing now.
cards.section: Semelparity, iteroparity and the cost of reproduction

cards.front: In laboratory female Drosophila melanogaster, dietary restriction lengthens life and lowers egg laying. What add-back experiment showed that long life did not require low reproduction?
cards.back: Single nutrients were added back to the restricted diet. With methionine alone, egg laying rose to the fully fed level and lifespan did not shorten.
cards.why: The link ran through the balance of particular nutrients, not one shared budget.
cards.quote: With methionine alone, fecundity (the number of eggs laid) rose to the fully fed level and lifespan did not shorten.
cards.section: Semelparity, iteroparity and the cost of reproduction

cards.front: Why does the Drosophila methionine add-back result give no basis for advice about human diet or fasting?
cards.back: It is one species studied in the laboratory; it says nothing about human diet, fasting or supplements.
cards.quote: This is one species in the laboratory, and it gives no basis for any advice about human diet, fasting or supplements.
cards.section: Semelparity, iteroparity and the cost of reproduction

cards.front: In population ecology, what do r and K stand for?
cards.back: r is the maximal intrinsic rate of increase, growth per individual per unit time when nothing limits it. K is the carrying capacity, the population size the environment can sustain.
cards.quote: r is the maximal intrinsic rate of increase, the rate at which a population grows per individual per unit time when nothing limits it.
cards.section: r and K, then the fast-slow continuum

cards.front: K is the {{c1::carrying capacity}}, the population size the environment can sustain.
cards.quote: K is the carrying capacity, the population size the environment can sustain.
cards.section: r and K, then the fast-slow continuum

cards.front: In Pianka's r/K scheme, what should r-selection and K-selection each favour, and where?
cards.back: r-selection: early reproduction and little investment per offspring, where populations often grow freely. K-selection: delayed reproduction and more investment per offspring, where populations sit near K.
cards.why: Pianka called these two ends of a spectrum, not a true dichotomy.
cards.quote: early reproduction and little investment in each offspring where populations often grow freely (r-selection)
cards.section: r and K, then the fast-slow continuum

cards.front: A species matures early and makes many small offspring. Why does this not show it is under r-selection?
cards.back: Other selective regimes can produce the same bundle of traits. The r/K scheme is best read as contrasting predictions, not a filing system.
cards.quote: A species with early maturity and many small offspring has not thereby been shown to be under r-selection
cards.section: r and K, then the fast-slow continuum

cards.front: Trinidad guppies are moved from a site where the main predator eats mostly adults to one where the main predator eats mostly juveniles. Predict how age at maturity and offspring size evolve.
cards.back: Later maturity at a larger size, and fewer, larger offspring. Descendants showed this within 11 years (an estimated 30 to 60 generations).
cards.why: Shifting deaths from adults to young favours waiting and investing more in each offspring, as theory about age-specific mortality predicts.
cards.quote: the introduced population had evolved later maturity at a larger size and fewer, larger offspring, as theory about age-specific mortality predicts.
cards.section: r and K, then the fast-slow continuum

cards.front: The Trinidad guppy transplant tests what, and why can it not show that predation alone caused the evolved change?
cards.back: It tests who dies at what age, not r and K. The move also changed density and food, so predation was not isolated; crowding may matter as well.
cards.quote: The move also changed density and food (Reznick and colleagues, 2001), so it did not isolate predation alone
cards.section: r and K, then the fast-slow continuum

cards.front: The modern descendant of r/K is the {{c1::fast-slow continuum}}: across species, early maturity, high annual fecundity and short life tend to go together, as do the opposites.
cards.quote: The modern descendant of r/K is the fast-slow continuum: across species, early maturity, high annual fecundity and short life tend to go together
cards.section: r and K, then the fast-slow continuum

cards.front: Long-term individual records from 17 bird and mammal species (2023) showed one main fast-slow axis across species. What did they show within the sampled populations?
cards.back: Individual differences mostly did not line up with that axis. A pattern among species cannot be assumed to hold for individuals.
cards.quote: Within the sampled populations, though, individual differences mostly did not line up with that axis.
cards.section: r and K, then the fast-slow continuum

cards.front: Using acquisition and allocation, explain why a fast-slow axis that holds across species can fail among individuals of one population.
cards.back: Individuals differ in intake. Those that take in more can breed more and also survive better, so within a population reproduction and survival need not trade off visibly, even though each individual faces a trade-off.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that differences in intake move individuals along both axes at once.
cards.quote: Because individuals differ in what they take in, a natural correlation can hide a trade-off

cards.front: In a model where reproduction R = split × intake and self-maintenance S = intake − R, all birds have equal intake but differ in split. What sign does the natural correlation between R and S take?
cards.back: Negative: the cloud slopes down, because each bird's split moves it along the same downward line.
cards.why: Only large variation in intake, relative to split, tilts the cloud up.
cards.quote: With equal intakes it slopes down.
cards.section: Testing a trade-off: correlation versus manipulation

cards.front: In a wild bird population, females that naturally lay larger clutches also survive better. Does this refute a cost of reproduction? Explain.
cards.back: No. If birds differ a lot in how much they acquire, high-intake birds can afford both larger clutches and better survival, so the cloud slopes up even though, for each bird, more on eggs leaves less for itself.
cards.quote: Differences in intake move birds out along both axes, tilting the cloud up
cards.section: Testing a trade-off: correlation versus manipulation

cards.front: Why is randomly changing breeding effort (for example, enlarging broods) a stronger test of a trade-off than a natural correlation, and what are its limits?
cards.back: Random assignment balances parent quality and intake, so a difference reflects the manipulation. Limits: the balance holds only on average, so differences carry sampling uncertainty, and it does not freeze intake (parents may forage harder).
cards.quote: changing breeding effort at random is the stronger test.

cards.front: Besides adult survival, where else can a cost of reproduction show up?
cards.back: In later breeding and in offspring quality.
cards.quote: survival is only one place a cost can show (later breeding and offspring quality are others)

cards.front: A 2025 meta-analysis of bird studies compared experimental brood enlargement with natural variation in clutch size, scaled to each species' average clutch. What opposite results did it find?
cards.back: Experimental enlargement lowered survival, while naturally larger clutches were associated with higher survival.
cards.why: The manipulation reveals the cost; natural variation in intake hides it.
cards.quote: Scaled to each species' average clutch, experimental enlargement lowered survival, while naturally larger clutches were associated with higher survival.
cards.section: Testing a trade-off: correlation versus manipulation

cards.front: In the 2025 bird meta-analysis, the raw per-chick effect of brood enlargement on survival had a 95% confidence interval that included zero. What can and cannot be concluded?
cards.back: The data cannot tell no average cost from a modest one, so a claim like "each extra egg costs X% survival" is not supported.
cards.quote: On the raw per-chick scale, though, the 95% confidence interval included zero
cards.section: Testing a trade-off: correlation versus manipulation

cards.front: Skylarks carrying an added load (about 10% of body mass) were compared with controls. In first broods, 19 of 25 control nests and 8 of 17 handicapped nests succeeded. Give the difference in nest success in percentage points and as a relative reduction.
cards.back: 19/25 = 76.0%; 8/17 = 47.1%. Difference: −28.9 percentage points. Relative reduction: (0.76 − 0.4706) / 0.76 = 38.1%.
cards.quote: In first broods, 19 of 25 control nests succeeded and 8 of 17 handicapped nests did.
cards.section: Testing a trade-off: correlation versus manipulation

cards.front: When comparing a treated rate with a control rate, what is the difference between a percentage-point difference and a percent (relative) change?
cards.back: Percentage points compare the two rates directly; percent measures the change against the control rate.
cards.quote: Percentage points compare two rates directly; percent measures the change against the control rate.
cards.section: Testing a trade-off: correlation versus manipulation

cards.front: In an invented experiment, 30 of 50 control nests and 20 of 50 treated nests fledge young. Give the difference in percentage points and the relative reduction.
cards.back: Rates are 60% and 40%: a drop of 20 percentage points. Relative reduction = (0.60 − 0.40) / 0.60 = 33.3%.
cards.quote: relative reduction = (control rate − treated rate) / control rate
cards.section: Testing a trade-off: correlation versus manipulation

cards.front: Handicapped skylark nests averaged 1.2 fledglings and controls 2.0, but successful nests fledged 2.6 young in both groups. Where must the whole fledgling deficit have come from?
cards.back: From nests that failed outright, not from smaller broods in successful nests.
cards.why: This locates the deficit, not its cause; the study did not show why those nests failed.
cards.quote: Successful nests fledged 2.6 young in both groups.
cards.section: Testing a trade-off: correlation versus manipulation

cards.front: What is a P value?
cards.back: The chance, if the treatment did nothing and the statistical model holds, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed.
cards.quote: A P value is the chance, if the treatment did nothing and the statistical model holds, of a result at least this extreme.
cards.section: Testing a trade-off: correlation versus manipulation

cards.front: In a skylark handicap study, nest success gave P = 0.055 and fledglings per nest gave P = 0.042. How should these be read?
cards.back: A 0.05 cutoff calls only the second significant, but the strength of evidence is nearly the same; treating one as an effect and the other as none overstates the difference.
cards.quote: a conventional 0.05 cutoff calls only the second significant, though the strength of evidence is nearly the same.
cards.section: Testing a trade-off: correlation versus manipulation

cards.front: In a skylark handicap study, adult return was 62.5% (handicapped) against 75% (controls), on 16 birds per group, and the difference was not significant. Does this show the handicap had no survival cost?
cards.back: No. With so few birds, "not significant" is weak evidence of no cost. A true drop from 75% to 50% would be detected only about one time in five.
cards.quote: Return was measured on only 16 birds per group (62.5% against 75%)
cards.section: Testing a trade-off: correlation versus manipulation

cards.front: Skylark pairs were assigned alternately to carry a harness plus extra load or nothing at all. Name two design weaknesses that limit what the study can conclude.
cards.back: Harness and load cannot be separated without a harness-only group. Alternation is not random: whoever assigns the next pair can predict its treatment.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's rule that only random assignment balances parent quality, and that each factor needs its own control.
cards.quote: And alternation is not random: whoever assigns the next pair can predict its treatment.
cards.section: Testing a trade-off: correlation versus manipulation

cards.front: Female seed beetles kept three to a container got either 5 or 40 unused beans each (the rest already used), then plenty of beans. Restricted females lived slightly shorter. Why does this not yet show that delaying reproduction costs lifespan?
cards.back: Confounds: three females sharing 15 usable beans means intense competition for laying sites; used beans may cue poor hosts; and the shorter life may come from the laying burst after release, not the delay.
cards.quote: with three females sharing 15 usable beans it also means intense competition among them for laying sites.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A crossed seed-beetle design varies usable beans per female (5 or 40, total beans constant) and females per container (one or several). Which results would point to the delay itself, to competition, or to the laying burst as the cost?
cards.back: Delay: few beans shorten life even for solitary females. Competition: more females shorten life, most when usable beans are scarce. Burst: gradually released females outlive those released all at once.
cards.quote: If delay itself is costly, low bean number shortens life even for solitary females.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a seed-beetle trade-off experiment, why record offspring reaching adulthood rather than only eggs laid, and why would a correlation between eggs and lifespan not settle the question?
cards.back: Eggs are not realized fitness. And females that acquired more can both lay more and live longer, so the correlation can be positive despite a cost.
cards.quote: the number of offspring that reach adulthood (eggs are not realized fitness)
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: When timing matters, as with age at first breeding, why does theory often use population growth rate rather than lifetime reproductive success as the fitness measure?
cards.back: Young produced early start breeding sooner, which lifetime totals ignore. Which measure is right depends on how the population is regulated.
cards.quote: theory often uses the population growth rate instead of lifetime reproductive success, because young produced early start breeding sooner.
cards.section: Which measure of fitness?

cards.front: What is Cole's paradox in the break-even rule b₁ − b₂ = p / c?
cards.back: When adult and juvenile survival are equal (p = c), the rule gives 1: one extra offspring would let a once-breeder match a repeat breeder.
cards.quote: When p = c the break-even rule gives 1: one extra offspring would match a repeat breeder, Cole's paradox.
cards.section: Cole's paradox and the shape of the trade-off

cards.front: How does the shape of the trade-off between reproduction and adult survival decide whether the best split is all-or-nothing or in between?
cards.back: If each extra unit of reproduction lowers survival by the same amount (a straight line), the best split is all or nothing. If the cost bites only at high effort, a middle split can win.
cards.quote: if the cost bites only at high effort, a middle split can win.
cards.section: Cole's paradox and the shape of the trade-off

cards.front: Why does the guppy transplant not test the textbook rule "more extrinsic mortality selects earlier maturity", and why is that rule not unconditional?
cards.back: The move changed which ages died, so it does not test the rule. In Dańko and colleagues' model, extra deaths striking all ages alike left allocation unchanged, selected earlier maturity, or selected later maturity, depending on how crowding acted.
cards.why: Crowding reducing survival evenly: no change; reducing fertility: earlier; reducing production rate: later.
cards.quote: The guppy move changed which ages died, so it does not test the textbook rule
cards.section: Extrinsic mortality and the three-case model
